claim: Wolfe plants each clue exactly once and refuses to repeat it, on the principle that a clue told five times is written for someone dumber than the reader.
source: Jordan 1992 interview (Shadows of the New Sun)
quote: I try not to leave a clue more than once

verdict.trueWording: 'I try not to leave a clue more than once ... if you tell me five times then I feel that you are writing for somebody that is a lot dumber than I am' (p.121).
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.121. Both limbs on the page; he also says 'So I try and leave my clues once.' Only softening: he says 'I try not to', a shade less absolute than the claim's 'refuses'.

claim: He says he leaves all the clues a reader will need and often more, because in real detection the work is finding more clues, not reasoning harder from a few.
quote: very little of it consists of reasoning from clues

verdict.trueWording: 'generally try and leave all the clues that I think the reader is going to require, sometimes more than they require' + 'very little of it consists of reasoning from clues and the great majority of it consists of finding more clues' (p.121).
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. Surplus-of-clues limb and the real-detection reason are both explicit, the latter framed as 'actual police work' / 'a real life situation'.

claim: Wolfe denies writing perspectival novels where confusion is the point: the clues are there, the puzzles are meant to be solved, and superficial confusion is simply how life looks before you think about it.
quote: Life seen superficially has very little pattern to it.

verdict.trueWording: 'Everything may be confusing but that is how things are... Life seen superficially has very little pattern to it.' (p.127)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (page reads '...pattern to it. There is a lot of confusion'). The 'clues are there / puzzles the reader is supposed to figure out / not that type of novel' formulation is Jordan's question, which Wolfe affirms with 'Yes' and then elaborates in his own words: 'It is not true that you can't get through the confusion and figure out certain things.' Attribution by assent, not by his own sentence.

claim: In Castleview different characters see the same unexplained thing as cowboys, Arthurian knights or a spaceship, modelled on anomaly reports where two witnesses describe a third thing differently.
quote: two witnesses who have very different stories

verdict.trueWording: 'When you research these anomalous stories and accounts you get this sort of thing. You get two witnesses who have very different stories depending on how they perceived some third thing that we don't know what it was. So I tried to show it like that.' (p.126)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. The cowboys/knights/spaceship enumeration is Jordan's question ('cowboys and Indians... Arthur and his knights... a spaceship'), which Wolfe adopts with 'So I tried to show it like that', and the Castleview context is explicit on the same page.

feature: supernatural premise to license memory's vividness
claim: Wolfe made Weer a dead man rather than a reminiscing old man so the remembered rooms could be re-created with a strength ordinary reminiscence could not justify.
quote: lend to the memories certain supernatural strengths

verdict.trueWording: 'Because I wanted to lend to the memories certain supernatural strengths that an old man thinking over his life wouldn't have. I wanted to do the rooms as re-creations of rooms that he had known as a very young man... I could not have gotten with just reminiscence.' (p.115)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and every limb on the page: dead man rather than reminiscing old man (Jordan's question, answered directly), the re-created rooms, and the strength plain reminiscence could not justify.

feature: ghost making sense of his life
claim: He conceived Peace not as purgatory but as a ghost trying to make sense of his own life, and accepts purgatory as another way of saying the same thing.
quote: a ghost trying to make sense of his own life

verdict.trueWording: 'That is not the way I conceived it when I wrote it. I conceived it more that he was a ghost trying to make sense of his own life. And I think that is another way of saying that.' (p.116)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. Both limbs hold, with a nuance the claim keeps: to 'is Weer in Purgatory working toward peace?' he first answers 'Yeah, I think probably he is', then distinguishes conception from purgatory and accepts purgatory as 'another way of saying that'.

claim: The Soldier books are built to show the problems of a genuinely good man who cannot remember, which Wolfe maps onto a decent society that has no awareness of its history.
quote: a genuinely good man who can't remember

verdict.trueWording: 'The book really is intended to show the problems faced by a genuinely good man who can't remember. Because it seems to me that is the problem of our society... our society has no memory because it has no awareness of history.' (p.118)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and the society mapping explicit ('We have a genuinely good society... quite decent individuals'; 'this America blundering around on the world stage more or less as Latro does'). Page says singular 'The book' (Soldier of Arete under discussion) where the claim says 'The Soldier books'.

feature: writing the pagan world from inside its belief
claim: For the Soldier books he wrote the ancient world as the pagans wrote about it rather than through the rationalist modern historian, so gods appear as the characters expected them to.
quote: as the pagans themselves wrote about it

verdict.trueWording: 'what I tried to do was to write about that pagan world as the pagans themselves wrote about it. If we read modern historians we are reading a very rationalistic viewpoint...' (p.117)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim; the rationalist-historian contrast is spelled out at length. The third limb is on the page too, via the Acts example: 'They are mistaken for Zeus and Hermes in human form because people in those days expected that you could see Zeus and Hermes in human form', prefaced by 'I think that the gods of paganism were real.'

claim: Wolfe says he used the memory-palace system of Simonides in the Soldier books.
quote: made use of the memory palace system

verdict.trueWording: 'I am familiar with the memory palace concept, which originally derives from Simonides, a Greek poet of the fifth century B.C... I have made use of the memory palace system in the Soldier books, of course.' (p.107)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim; Simonides and the Soldier books both named in the same answer. He adds that he has heard of Yates's The Art of Memory but not read it.

claim: He says symbolic details arrive as local impulses ('that's neat; I'll do that') and denies the books are allegories.
quote: The book isn't intended as an allegory.

verdict.trueWording: 'Every once in a while you say, "Gee, that's neat; I'll do that." And you do it. I wasn't writing the whole book that way. The book isn't intended as an allegory.' (p.118)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim including the period. The impulse phrasing on the page is 'Gee, that's neat; I'll do that.' The denial is singular ('The book') where the claim generalises to 'the books'; he separately denies allegory for Free Live Free on p.128 ('I wasn't trying to write allegory').

claim: Wolfe claims he can identify a writer from a paragraph or two and could write imitation Shakespeare or Lewis that passes, a self-described knack for voice.
quote: I am a good imitator.

verdict.trueWording: 'I could almost invariably identify the writer from the first paragraph or two... And I am a good imitator. I could write imitation Shakespeare that you would think was probably legitimate Shakespeare... I have sort of a knack for doing that sort of thing.' (p.103)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and every limb explicit, including the Lewis limb ('I could write much better imitation C. S. Lewis than a lot of this supposedly posthumous stuff') and the self-described knack. The paragraph-or-two identification is set in a writers' chain letter, alongside 'I am pretty good at spotting styles'.

claim: He describes the Severian books as in part his decision to rewrite The Dying Earth from his own standpoint, openly acknowledging Vance and Clark Ashton Smith.
quote: rewrite The Dying Earth from my own standpoint

verdict.trueWording: 'Was Jack Vance's style an influence on the style of the Severian novels?' - 'Oh, I'm sure... A lot of that was my deciding to rewrite The Dying Earth from my own standpoint' (p.103); 'I have never concealed a debt to Jack Vance and a debt to Clark Ashton Smith' (p.104).
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on p.103. 'In part' matches 'A lot of that'. The Clark Ashton Smith acknowledgment sits just over the page break on p.104, not on p.103 as the page field implies.

claim: He reads scriptural images (the apple, the sky rolled up) as figurative language giving a general idea to an audience unable to grasp the actuality, a model for conveying meaning in pictures.
quote: figurative language to try to give a general idea

verdict.trueWording: 'We don't know what is really meant by the world coming to an end, and God rolling up the sky like a carpet and all that. It is all picturesque language, figurative language to try to give a general idea to an audience that would not be capable of understanding the actuality.' (p.129)
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. The apple limb follows immediately: 'It is like the Genesis story. I don't believe in a literal "apple"... but if you have to explain to a bunch of primitives how men differ from animals... this is a pretty good way to do it.' 'In pictures' tracks the page's own 'picturesque language'.

claim: Any narrator who is a person inside the story is going to be unreliable; five or six honest courtroom witnesses to one event all report different things.
quote: the narrator is damn well going to be unreliable

verdict.trueWording: "then the narrator is damn well going to be unreliable"
verdict.note: Raw PDF text extracted with pypdf from gwern.net copy (Shadows of the New Sun ch.12, p.169). Quote appears word for word. Both limbs on page: narration by 'this person in the story' entails unreliability, and 'Ask any courtroom lawyer about examining five or six different witnesses to the same event. The five or six witnesses are all trying to tell the truth, but they have all seen different things.' 'Honest' = 'all trying to tell the truth'.

feature: unattributed dialogue by idiolect and content
claim: Speakers in crowded Long Sun scenes are identified without tags by characteristic phrases or mistakes and by each saying only what that character would say in that circumstance.
quote: saying something that only Maytera Marble would say

verdict.trueWording: "she is saying something that only Maytera Marble would say"
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.168. Quote verbatim. Interviewer's question supplies the crowded-scene limb ('scenes with a number of characters all speaking in turn without being identified'); Wolfe gives both mechanisms: 'certain characteristic phrases or mistakes, or whatever, that will identify him as the speaker' and the circumstance test ('the speech that... Maytera Marble makes under a certain circumstance, is not the speech that Blood would make').

claim: The more complex the story, the clearer its narrative structure must be; shaken up, a ten-thousand-part machine is just a box of junk.
quote: it isn't complex, it's simply confused

verdict.trueWording: "or it isn't complex, it's simply confused"; 10,000 parts shaken = "a box of junk"
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.169. Quote verbatim. Machine limb verbatim too: 'If you have a machine with 10,000 parts and you shake them up in a box, what you have is a box of junk.' One hedge worth recording: Wolfe answers 'It's almost that it has to be', slightly softer than the claim's flat 'must be', but the proposition is his and affirmed.

claim: He finds the Latin or Greek word for the thing he needs, then searches unabridged dictionaries on the assumption that someone once anglicised it, often finding an 18th-century citation.
quote: someone will have anglicised this term

verdict.trueWording: "on the assumption that someone will have anglicised this term as a new word"
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.173-174. Quote verbatim. Every limb present: 'looking up the Latin or Greek word that corresponds to something you need a word for, and then going back to unabridged dictionaries...' and 'very often you find that somebody did indeed do that, and it crops up in the Oxford dictionary for a citation in the 18th century or whatever.'

claim: In Fifth Head the story attributed to John V. Marsch is actually written by the shadowchild who replaced him, a trick Wolfe concedes is New Wave.
quote: not actually written by John V. Marsch

verdict.trueWording: "not actually written by John V. Marsch, but by the shadowchild who has replaced" him
verdict.note: Raw PDF p.169. Quote verbatim. New Wave limb doubly supported: Wolfe calls it 'the rather tricky thing, which I suppose is New Wave' and then, after the interviewer supplies the title, 'That's New Wave.' 'Concedes' is fair - he had just minimised his New Wave membership.

feature: diversity of registers within one world
claim: Wolfe rejects monocultured SF worlds as mental sloth, noting that in one big city people at different social levels already speak almost different languages.
quote: Mental sloth more than anything else.

verdict.trueWording: "I think it's mostly laziness. Mental sloth more than anything else."
verdict.note: Raw PDF pp.172-173. Quote verbatim. Big-city limb verbatim: 'If you look at a big city, you discover that, on various levels of society, people are talking in ways that are almost different languages already.' The monoculture-criticism limb is established in the question ('you have in the past criticised sf works that depict monocultured worlds') and affirmed by the answer.

feature: revision turns synopsis into hard facts
claim: Wolfe often first writes synopsis and in revision lengthens it, turning generalities into hard facts and making each speaker talk as she talks.
quote: I turned generalities into hard facts.

verdict.trueWording: "I turned generalities into hard facts. I made India talk the way she talks."
verdict.note: Raw HTML fetched from clarkesworldmagazine.com (HTTP 200) and de-tagged locally; no summarizer. Quote verbatim. Synopsis limb: 'Often I tend to write synopsis. When I do, I have to flesh it out in revision.' Lengthening limb: interviewer notes 'you made the second version longer' and Wolfe answers 'It's longer, but it has a lot more meat.'

claim: He forbids himself sentences like 'Nick was a bad man and a cruel man' and must instead show Nick being bad within the story.
quote: Easy writing makes damned hard reading.

verdict.trueWording: "'Nick was a bad man and a cruel man.' That's easy. I know I can't say it at all."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML. Quote verbatim, though on the page Wolfe attributes it to another ('Long ago somebody said, "Easy writing makes damned hard reading."') - the claim does not assert authorship, so no limb fails. Show-don't-state limb verbatim: 'I have to show [Nick] being bad and cruel in the context of the story.'

claim: He stops when he can no longer tell whether changes improve the piece, usually after four drafts; a fifth that reverts to the second is a bad sign.
quote: A fifth draft may find me reverting

verdict.trueWording: "A fifth draft may find me reverting to the second or the third, and that's a bad sign."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML. Quote verbatim. Stopping-rule limb verbatim: 'There comes a point at which I'm no longer sure that what I'm doing is improving the piece. That's when I stop working on it and send it in. Usually - not always, but usually - I get there after four drafts.' Page says reverting to the second OR THIRD; the claim's 'second' is a subset, not a contradiction.

claim: Dialogue must entertain, forward the plot and characterize the speaker at once, and sound like what that speaker would say to that person then.
quote: Dialogue is action.

verdict.trueWording: "It must entertain the reader, forward the plot, and characterize the speaker."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML. Quote 'Dialogue is action.' verbatim as its own line. Simultaneity limb: 'All pretty much at the same time.' Naturalness limb verbatim: 'it must sound natural - that is, like something that speaker might say at that time to that person.'

claim: Even unimportant characters must speak differently from one another; students reject this because everybody sounds alike to them.
quote: The butler mustn't sound like the footman

verdict.trueWording: "The butler mustn't sound like the footman, even though neither is an important character."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML. Quote verbatim. Student limb verbatim: 'This is one of those truths that students reject out of hand. They reject it because everybody sounds alike. / To them.' - the page's line break makes 'To them' the sting, which the claim renders correctly.

claim: Like poetry and song, fiction demands the concrete; he contrasts an abstract shipwreck summary with a ballad naming the ship, the cargo and the shoal.
quote: fiction demands the concrete

verdict.trueWording: "Like poetry and song, fiction demands the concrete."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML. Quote verbatim. The contrast is on the page: abstract version 'The vessel, bearing fuel to the New World, met with misfortune shortly before its arrival'; ballad names ship ('the Nightingale'), cargo ('Twenty-one days from Clyde in coal') and shoal ('he drowned on the hard-rock shoal'). All three nouns of the claim check out.

feature: expectation and satisfaction as story engine
claim: A short story works by engendering expectations and satisfying them; he told a student to post a sign reading 'I AM GOING TO TELL YOU SOMETHING COOL'.
quote: engendering expectations and satisfying them

verdict.trueWording: "By engendering expectations and satisfying them."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML, answering 'In general terms, how does a short story work?' Quote verbatim. Sign limb verbatim including capitalisation: 'I told a student once to letter a sign and put it where he'd see it when he wrote: "I AM GOING TO TELL YOU SOMETHING COOL."'

claim: Realistic fiction leaves out far too much of human experience; fantasy is nearer the truth.
quote: Realistic fiction leaves out far, far too much.

verdict.trueWording: "Because fantasy is nearer the truth, that's all... Realistic fiction leaves out far, far too much."
verdict.note: Raw Clarkesworld HTML. Quote verbatim. Both limbs in one answer; the human-experience limb is carried by the adjacent 'How true is that story for the bulk of humankind?' Claim's ordering is reversed from the page's, which does not affect support.

claim: Style should suit the story; a wrong style is comic for ten pages, and the narrator's voice is inseparable from style.
quote: the style should suit the story

verdict.trueWording: "Other than that, the style should suit the story."
verdict.note: Clarkesworld 2008 fetched raw (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim. All limbs on page: 'Imagine The Wings of the Dove as told by Huck Finn. It would be funny for ten pages, but . . .' and 'the author's voice, or the narrator's, it's so closely linked to style that I see no point in discussing it separately.'

feature: narrator may comment; author may not
claim: First person puts the reader inside the story and lets the narrator comment on actions, whereas authorial comment is usually ruinously bad.
quote: it's usually ruinously bad

verdict.trueWording: "If the author comments from his viewpoint, it's usually ruinously bad."
verdict.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim. Page: 'When you have a first person narrator, you are much more into the story. Also, the first person narrator can comment from his viewpoint on actions.' Note the page's 'you are much more into the story' is the writer's vantage as much as the reader's; the claim's 'puts the reader inside the story' is a mild gloss but consistent with the answer's contrast to third person distance.

claim: Narrators are either openly unreliable or pretend to be totally reliable, but all are unreliable because people write books and people cannot be trusted.
quote: narrators that pretend to be totally reliable

verdict.trueWording: "they are always unreliable because people are writing books and people can't be trusted"
verdict.note: Clarkesworld 2015 raw. Quote verbatim within: 'There are narrators that are openly unreliable and there are narrators that pretend to be totally reliable. But they are always unreliable because people are writing books and people can't be trusted, you know?' Every limb supported.

claim: Characterization is done only by showing the character thinking, speaking and acting characteristically, never by telling the reader about him.
quote: You simply show it and shut up.

verdict.trueWording: "You do not characterize by telling the reader about the character... You simply show it and shut up."
verdict.note: Black Gate 2010 raw (HTTP 200). Item 4 of Wolfe's numbered advice list: 'You do not characterize by telling the reader about the character. You do it by showing the character thinking, speaking and acting in a characteristic way. You simply show it and shut up.' Every limb verbatim.

claim: Do not start a story without an ending in mind; the ending may change but there must always be a destination.
quote: you should always have a destination

verdict.trueWording: "Do not start a story unless you have an ending in mind."
verdict.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Item 5: 'Do not start a story unless you have an ending in mind. You can change the story's ending if you wish, but you should always have a destination.' Quote verbatim; both limbs (ending may change; always a destination) on page.

claim: He does almost no research before writing and fills in world details as he reaches them, researching as he goes (what Greeks ate for breakfast: nothing).
quote: I do research while I'm writing the book.

verdict.trueWording: "how much research I do before I start writing. The answer is, almost none."
verdict.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim. Page continues: 'If it's a book on Ancient Greece, what is it about Ancient Greece that I need to know? What did Ancient Greeks eat for breakfast?' and, asked, 'They didn't eat breakfast!' — supporting research-as-you-go and the breakfast parenthesis.

claim: In 'The Tree Is My Hat' the ex-wife's name Mary Christmas is never stated; the reader finds it out by deduction.
quote: you find out by deduction

verdict.trueWording: "the ex-wife... is named Mary Christmas. I never say that - you find out by deduction"
verdict.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim; the page spells the title 'The Tree is My Hat' (lower-case 'is'), a typographic difference only. All limbs supported.

claim: Wolfe says the storytelling contest in the third New Sun volume is strictly padding added when the publisher split the book.
quote: a storytelling contest that's strictly padding

verdict.trueWording: "If you look in the third book, you will find a storytelling contest that's strictly padding."
verdict.note: Black Gate 2010 raw. Quote verbatim. The split limb is supported immediately before: 'My publisher thought that I should divide it into two books and build each book up... That's what I did.'

claim: Wolfe attributes the shorter paragraphs and looser tone of his later books to criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex, after which he decided to loosen up.
quote: criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex

verdict.trueWording: "criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex... 'Well, I'll loosen up.'"
verdict.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw (HTTP 200, full article text retrieved, section 'EDITING AND WRITING'). Quote verbatim inside: 'It's that I've gotten so much criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex and hard to get into and all this stuff. And I thought, "Well, I'll loosen up."' The shorter-paragraphs/looser-tone description is the interviewer's, which Wolfe re-explains ('It's not that, really') by the criticism — exactly the attribution the claim makes.

feature: difficulty as duty to the reader
claim: He sets himself hard technical challenges with narrators because an author who makes everything easy for himself bores the reader.
quote: you bore the reader

verdict.trueWording: "If you make everything easy for yourself as an author, you bore the reader."
verdict.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw, section 'UNRELIABLE NARRATORS AND CRAFT'. Interviewer: 'With your narrators, you set yourself difficult technical challenges.' Wolfe's answer is the quoted line. Both limbs supported.

feature: ghost who does not know he is dead
claim: Weer's unreliability is that he is a ghost, and ghosts often do not realize they are dead.
quote: Ghosts often don't realize they're dead.

verdict.trueWording: "He's a ghost. Ghosts often don't realize they're dead."
verdict.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw, same section. Quote verbatim (typographic apostrophes normalized). The interviewer names Weer as 'unreliable in this particular sense: he's dead, and doesn't know it', and Wolfe affirms 'He's a ghost.'

feature: narrator talking himself into a false identity
claim: Marsch in Fifth Head knows he is not a real Earthman but is trying to talk himself into believing he is.
quote: trying to talk himself into believing that he is

verdict.trueWording: "He knows he's not a real Earthman, but he's trying to talk himself into believing that he is."
verdict.note: MIT Technology Review 2014 raw, same section, answering whether John Marsch understands he is really V.R.T. Quote verbatim; every limb on the page.

claim: A naive observer is more interesting because he gives only what he has seen, whereas adult witnesses cannot separate what they saw from what it means.
quote: he's just giving you what he has seen

verdict.trueWording: "he's just giving you what he has seen"
verdict.note: Raw MIT Tech Review page fetched with a browser UA (200, 468KB). Wolfe: "I think a naive observer is more interesting to read because he's just giving you what he has seen. If you've ever listened to people giving testimony at a trial, they are almost incapable of distinguishing between what they have actually seen or heard and their opinions of what it means." Quote verbatim. Wording note: the page says "people giving testimony at a trial", not literally "adult witnesses" — the child/adult contrast is the question's frame (young narrators, "what Maisie knew"); substance of the limb is fully supported.

feature: perfect memory and daily amnesia as inverse designs
claim: Having built Severian to forget nothing, Wolfe built Latro from a real brain injury to forget everything.
quote: let's do one of these guys who forgets everything

verdict.trueWording: "In Severian, I had created a character who forgot nothing"
verdict.note: Same page. Wolfe: "I came across an article about a brain injury that is perfectly real [anterograde amnesia]... In Severian, I had created a character who forgot nothing. And I thought: let's do one of these guys who forgets everything." The interviewer frames it as "In the Soldier series you created a narrator who forgets everything at the end of every day"; the same page names Latro as the Soldier series narrator, so the Latro identification is page-supported. Quote verbatim.

claim: Every narrator is unreliable because each sees from his own standpoint and not another's.
quote: They're all unreliable. Well, we all are, aren't we?

verdict.trueWording: "You see things from your standpoint and not from... someone else"
verdict.note: Same page. Q: "A persistent theme of your writing is the unreliability of narrators." Wolfe: "They're all unreliable. Well, we all are, aren't we?" Then, to "Everyone's story is necessarily subjective": "You see things from your standpoint and not from the standpoint of someone else." Both limbs verbatim.

feature: epistolary entry with per-writer style shifts
claim: He recommends The Sorcerer's House as an entry point because the epistolary form helps readers, provided they accept the style changing with each letter writer.
quote: the style changes from one letter writer to another

verdict.trueWording: "It's an epistolary novel, and that seems to help people along"
verdict.note: Same page, EDITING AND WRITING section, answering how a Niven/Card/Brin reader should start Wolfe: "I think it's probably The Sorcerer's House. It's an epistolary novel, and that seems to help people along. So long as they don't get bothered by the fact that the style changes from one letter writer to another." Every limb verbatim.

claim: Military service teaches you to look at scenery as defensive positions, the perception behind Severian's line that war is a new geography.
quote: look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions

verdict.trueWording: "You learn to look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions"
verdict.note: Same page, WAR AND RELIGION section. The interviewer quotes Severian's passage ("War is not a new experience; it is a new world ... Even its geography is new, because it is a geography in which insignificant hills and hollows are lifted to the importance of cities") and Wolfe's whole reply is the quoted line. The claim's link between the Severian passage and the perception is by direct adjacency (reply to that quoted passage), not an explicit statement; the military framing is the section's own ("What military service does is rub off a lot of the pretense and self-deception").

claim: Wolfe learned prose from a college editor who blue-pencilled every word a sentence did not require, and he wrote the next story so it could not be cut.
quote: taking out every word the sentence

verdict.trueWording: "He's taking out every word the sentence doesn't require"
verdict.note: locusmag.com/2002/Issue09/GaimanWolfe.html fetched raw (200, 17KB; page uses a legacy charset so curly apostrophes render as replacement chars — normalized before matching). Wolfe on the student editor of The Commentator at Texas A&M: "he got a blue pencil, and he edited it there in front of me... 'I see what he's doing. He's taking out every word the sentence doesn't require. I'm going to write the next story so he can't do that.'" Also "I learned more from the student editor of The Commentator than I have ever learned from any other editor." All limbs supported.

claim: His definition of good literature is what an educated reader can read and reread with increased pleasure, and he refuses to write fiction that gives everything up on first reading.
quote: reread with increased pleasure

verdict.trueWording: "read by an educated reader, and reread with increased pleasure"
verdict.note: Same Locus page. Gaiman quotes Wolfe's own letter definition: "My definition of good literature is that which can be read by an educated reader, and reread with increased pleasure." On fiction that gives everything up first time, Wolfe: "Phooey! I don't want to write that kind of thing. Rats! I don't like it and it would bore me to write it and I'm not gonna write it." Both limbs supported; the definition is Wolfe's, quoted back to him by Gaiman.

claim: He will not adjudicate readers' theories about the text because he argues from presumed expertise on an unlevel field, and there is no sacredness to the text.
quote: no sacredness to the text

verdict.trueWording: "I am dealing from this position of presumed expertise"
verdict.note: Same Locus page: "too often people want me to go in and settle their argument. That's exactly what I should not do. I am dealing from this position of presumed expertise. We don't have a level playing field... There's no sacredness to the text." Every limb verbatim, including the Baker Street Irregulars analogy that carries it.

claim: Wolfe says readers will see things in the books he does not see consciously, and that he likes those things.
quote: I like those things.

verdict.trueWording: "You're going to see things in there that I don't see consciously"
verdict.note: Same Locus page: "And besides, I don't know everything to give it up. You're going to see things in there that I don't see consciously. I like those things." Quote and both limbs verbatim.

feature: Peace built on lies (Gaiman) vs. 'I never lie'
claim: Gaiman calls Wolfe the master of lying in fiction and says Peace is built on lies decipherable after three or four readings; Wolfe replies that he never lies.
quote: I never lie.

verdict.trueWording: "Peace is built on lies" / "I never lie."
verdict.note: Same Locus page. Gaiman: "I think Gene is the master of lying in fiction, both directly and indirectly. Peace is built on lies... After three or four times through that text, you begin to be able to say, 'I think he's lying about this or that.'" Wolfe's entire reply: "I never lie." All three limbs (master of lying, Peace built on lies, three or four readings, the reply) verbatim.

feature: fiction as assurance that things need not be as they are
claim: The most important thing fiction does is assure the reader that things need not be as they are now, which Wolfe names hope.
quote: the most important thing is hope

verdict.trueWording: "it assures the reader that things need not be as they are now"
verdict.note: Same Locus page. Q: "What's the most important thing about fiction?" Wolfe: "The most important thing is that it assures the reader that things need not be as they are now. In other words, the most important thing is hope." Every limb verbatim.

claim: Anything in a book must do several things at once (tone, plot, character); a 'pass the salt' line is waste unless said in a particular way or for a purpose.
quote: you really have to be doing several things at once

verdict.trueWording: "it's a waste unless it's said in some particular way"
verdict.note: locusmag.com/2011/03/gene-wolfe-engineering-the-future/ fetched raw (200, 163KB); page is the excerpts from the March 2011 Locus interview. Wolfe: "When you do anything in a book, you really have to be doing several things at once. You need to pique the tone of the book; to move the plot forward; to touch on the character of the person. If you've got a dinner scene where somebody says, 'Pass the salt,' it's a waste unless it's said in some particular way, or the character wants the salt for some special purpose." Every limb verbatim, tone/plot/character included.

claim: Wolfe denies his style has changed at all: he writes in a voice appropriate to the story he has to tell.
quote: I write in a voice appropriate to the story

verdict.trueWording: "My style hasn't changed at all"
verdict.note: Wayback capture 20020703232613 of sfsite.com/03b/gw124.htm fetched raw (200, 41KB); header confirms "A Magus Of Many Suns: An Interview With Gene Wolfe / An interview with Nick Gevers / January 2002". Wolfe: "My style hasn't changed at all. I write in a voice appropriate to the story I have to tell, that's all. I may be doing it a bit better now, or a bit worse; but that's always been the idea." Both limbs verbatim.

claim: A style becomes difficult only when it is not suited to what is being said; if it is the right style he likes it, if not he changes it.
quote: A style becomes difficult when it is not suited

verdict.trueWording: "I use the style suited to the story... If it isn't, I change it"
verdict.note: Same SF Site capture: "There really aren't any answers. I use the style suited to the story. If it's the right style for the story, I like it. If it isn't, I change it. A style becomes difficult when it is not suited to what is being said." Quote and both limbs verbatim. Wording note: the page says "becomes difficult when it is not suited"; the claim's "only when" is a (fair, context-consistent) tightening, not the page's word.

claim: Character speech comes from listening to what people actually say as well as what they mean; Remora and Incus are slight exaggerations of real people, and Oreb manages only two syllables.
quote: what they actually say as well as what they mean

verdict.trueWording: "Oreb can manage only two syllables"
verdict.note: Same SF Site capture: "I listen to people, what they actually say as well as what they mean, and how they say it. Both Patera Remora and Patera Incus speak as slight exaggerations of people I've met." And: "Oreb [the night chough, a talking bird] talks, but Oreb can manage only two syllables: 'Good bird! Watch out! Bad boy. Iron girl. Good Silk!'" All three limbs verbatim.

claim: For about half the first draft of Long Sun Wolfe did not know who was writing it, considered Maytera Marble, settled on Horn and rewrote accordingly.
quote: I didn't know who was writing

verdict.trueWording: "For about half the first draft, I didn't know who was writing The Book of the Long Sun, and considered various characters -- Maytera Marble, for example. I finally settled on Horn, and did the rewrites with that in mind."
verdict.note: Every limb verbatim on the SF Site page (Wayback 20020703232613): half the first draft, not knowing the writer, Maytera Marble as a considered candidate, settling on Horn, rewrites done with that in mind.

feature: third person would be dead on the page
claim: He chose Short Sun's interwoven narrators because telling it in third person would have been dead on the page; the difficulty was balancing storylines.
quote: it would have been dead there on the page

verdict.trueWording: "I could have done everything in third person, but it would have been dead there on the page. The chief difficulty was balancing the stories -- not letting one storyline run away with the book."
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. The interviewer's question frames the approach as the interweaving of past/present with uncertain narrator identities, so 'interwoven narrators' is the question's own wording. Minor nuance: Wolfe's primary stated reason is 'that was what I had to do to tell the story'; the third-person remark is his supporting contrast, exactly as the claim renders it.

feature: secondary narrators reconstruct honestly but fallibly
claim: Daisy, principal writer of the Whorl chapters, strings others' accounts into plausible incidents and has deliberately falsified nothing, leaving errors to ignorance not intent.
quote: She has deliberately falsified nothing.

verdict.trueWording: "Daisy is the principal writer of the storyline back on the Whorl... She has done her best to string the incidents together and make everything plausible. She has deliberately falsified nothing."
verdict.note: Quote and the first three limbs verbatim. The last limb ('errors to ignorance not intent') is the direct entailment of the question it answers -- 'Have Hoof, Hide, Daisy, and Vadsig got major details wrong, deliberately, or out of ignorance?' -- but note that Wolfe does not concede the one alleged error: on the godling's size he replies 'he is far too large if he is structured along familiar lines, but who said he was?'

claim: Asked directly whether Pig is a godling, Wolfe says certainly, since there are telltale signs all through the book.
quote: There are telltale signs all through the book.

verdict.trueWording: Q: "Is Pig a godling?" GW: "Certainly. There are telltale signs all through the book."
verdict.note: Direct question, direct answer, both verbatim; the interviewer's bracketed '[Hooray! But...]' confirms it was one of the deliberately blunt questions.

feature: the reader is expected to get it
claim: He is surprised readers missed the inhumi secret (they prey on us because we prey on each other), which he thought everyone would get.
quote: I thought that everyone would get it

verdict.trueWording: "If human beings did not prey on one another, the inhumi could not prey on us. That's all. It isn't complicated, and I thought that everyone would get it."
verdict.note: Quote verbatim; the parenthetical restates Wolfe's conditional as a causal, which the page supports. Surprise is carried by the following sentence: 'Maybe the thought of human beings not preying on their own kind is just too foreign.'

claim: Wolfe cites Roger Rabbit slipping the handcuffs 'only when it's funny' as the law binding writers: a gun on the wall in Act I must be fired.
quote: No, only when it's funny.

verdict.trueWording: Roger: "No, only when it's funny." -- "That is a profound expression of the law that governs all writers and performers... If there's a gun on the wall in Act I, it must be fired before the end of the play."
verdict.note: All three limbs verbatim: the Roger Rabbit handcuffs anecdote, the line as the law binding writers and performers, and the Act I gun.

feature: story built backward from an ending image
claim: He constructs a clued short story from one or more ideas and an ending image, answering the questions that image raises before writing.
quote: I have one or more ideas, and an ending

verdict.trueWording: "I have one or more ideas, and an ending -- a space ship takes off, and the blast fries someone who's been waiting outside. Who was that?... When I had answered those questions, I could write the story, and I did."
verdict.note: Verbatim, in answer to a question about his 'precisely-honed tales, with their wealth of subtle clues' and specifically 'In Glory Like Their Star'; 'clued' is the interviewer's descriptor, which Wolfe accepts ('Thanks. Thank you!') before giving the method.

claim: Gevers characterizes Wolfe's range as writing alternately with limpid simplicity and formidable baroque density of diction, in the service of oblique many-layered fictions.
quote: a formidable baroque density of diction

verdict.trueWording: "he possesses an extraordinary stylistic breadth, writing alternately with limpid simplicity and with a formidable baroque density of diction; and all this in the service of oblique, many-layered, endlessly surprising and beautifully structured fictions."
verdict.note: Verbatim in Gevers's own introduction (bylined 'An interview with Nick Gevers', Copyright 2002 Nick Gevers); attribution to Gevers rather than Wolfe is correct. The same paragraph is reproduced verbatim in the 2003 Infinity Plus introduction.

claim: Ambiguity is necessary in some of his stories and not in others; where present it contributes richness, but he doubts thematic closure is never attainable.
quote: Ambiguity is necessary in some of my stories, not in all.

verdict.trueWording: "Ambiguity is necessary in some of my stories, not in all. In those, it certainly contributes to the richness of the story. I doubt that thematic closure is never attainable."
verdict.note: All three limbs verbatim on the live infinityplus.co.uk page, answering Gevers's question about whether thematic closure is never attainable. Wolfe's 'I doubt that thematic closure is never attainable' is reproduced with its double negative intact.

claim: The Knight's narrator is a contemporary American because Wolfe needed someone from outside who would not have grown up hearing of the Aelf and Angrborn.
quote: who would not have heard about the Aelf

verdict.trueWording: "I felt I needed to bring in someone from outside, who would not have heard about the Aelf and Angrborn from childhood."
verdict.note: Verbatim, answering 'Why did you choose to make the narrator of The Knight a contemporary American?'; 'from childhood' is the page's wording for 'grown up hearing of'. Wolfe prefaces it with 'I've no good answer' before giving the reason.

feature: do not dumb down pivotal events
claim: Wolfe holds that people's pivotal life events as they actually occurred would not be believed, and that literature should not dumb reality down but smart it up.
quote: we don't dumb it down

verdict.trueWording: "if you were to tell me the pivotal events of your life, as they actually occurred, I wouldn't believe you" / "Let's write literature in which we don't dumb it down. Let's 'smart' it up."
verdict.note: Both limbs verbatim in the Baber interview (Wayback 20060208231553). The 'smart it up' sentence puts 'smart' in quotation marks on the page.

claim: Real complex character comes from people who are rotten only selectively, nice to their drinking buddies, unlike utopian or dystopian casts.
quote: most rotten people are only rotten selectively

verdict.trueWording: "most rotten people are only rotten selectively. They're not lousy and rotten to their kids, or they are, but they're nice to their drinking buddies."
verdict.note: Quote and the drinking-buddies limb verbatim. The utopian/dystopian contrast is the immediately preceding text ('Utopias in the utopian novels work because everyone is good and reasonable'; 'The dystopian novel... Everybody is lousy and rotten in all their relationships'), and the complex-character limb is Wolfe's next answer: Q 'So the goal is to make complex character?' GW 'I think that's what real human character is.'

feature: paper is paper: the concrete credo
claim: Against a materialist correspondent Wolfe insists a piece of paper is a piece of paper and cheese is cheese, the animal-level knowing that living and, by implication, fiction require.
quote: It is paper. It is cheese.

verdict.trueWording: "the one thing that we really can't get along without is the realization that a piece of paper is a piece of paper... That's what you've got to do to live on the animal level." / "Knowing what it is. It is paper. It is cheese."
verdict.note: Quote verbatim; the correspondent is verbatim 'a materialist philosophy student who used to write to me', and the cheese figure is the mouse's 'I know cheese'. The fiction application is flagged by the claim itself as 'by implication' and is contextual: the materialism exchange grows out of Wolfe calling literary realism 'a dumbed-down part of reality'. The page never states the fiction consequence outright.

feature: write a book, not a genre
claim: He defends mixing private eyes and witches in one SF novel because such people exist; he is not trying to write genres.
quote: I'm not trying to write genres

verdict.trueWording: "I'm not trying to write genres, I'm trying to write a book."
verdict.note: Verbatim, and both existence defences are on the page for Free Live Free: 'there are real private eyes. Look in the phone book' and 'I've had witches give me their business cards... They're real people.'

claim: Asked why he is drawn to deceptions that turn out to be true, Wolfe says it must be the unconscious hope that some of his will.
quote: the unconscious hope that some of mine will

verdict.trueWording: I'm sure it must be the unconscious hope that some of mine will.
verdict.note: Q2 on the page: 'What is his [Wolfe's] attraction to [pretences or deceptions that turn out to be true]? - I'm sure it must be the unconscious hope that some of mine will.' Quote matches word for word; both limbs (the question asked, the answer given) are on the page. The bracketed restorations of the abbreviated question are the editor's, as the page states up front.

claim: Scenes Horn could not have witnessed are sourced within the fiction (an unnamed kite builder; prayers written by Horn and Nettle who heard Silk pray), and Wolfe points to a page in Exodus.
quote: Please reread Exodus, p. 371.

verdict.trueWording: Please reread Exodus, p. 371.
verdict.note: Q21 asks about scenes 'hard to imagine Horn hearing about from witnesses'. Wolfe: 'Horn's information on the first came from the kite builder, who asked that his name not be used. Silk's prayers (etc.) were written by Horn and Nettle, who had heard him pray many times. Please reread Exodus, p. 371.' Every limb - unnamed kite builder, prayers written by Horn and Nettle who heard Silk pray, the Exodus page pointer - is present.

feature: happened / probably happened / must have happened
claim: Horn and Nettle tell what happened, what probably happened and what must have happened, in dramatic form; their account is necessarily subjective and they make mistakes.
quote: what probably happened, and what must have happened

verdict.trueWording: Horn and Nettle are doing their best to tell you what happened, what probably happened, and what must have happened, in dramatic form.
verdict.note: Q21a ('How trustworthy a narrator is Horn?'). The page continues: 'They are human beings, however, and make mistakes. (We all do, especially me.) Their account is subjective, necessarily, as all accounts are.' Quote exact; the subjectivity and mistake limbs both present.

claim: Wolfe concedes the Mint/Marble location swap in Exodus is his mistake; Langford notes readers had been reading subtleties into his least typos.
quote: they are my mistakes

verdict.trueWording: You're right, and they are my mistakes.
verdict.note: Q28 asks about Mint and Marble seeming to exchange places near the end of Exodus, deliberate or an auctorial/editorial mistake. Quote exact. The editorial aside is signed with initials - '[DRL: You can't imagine how relieved this made me! We read subtleties into Wolfe's least typos....]' - and the name Langford does not appear on cc77 itself; the publication's own index at ansible.uk/cc/ states 'Cloud Chamber is another bloody Langford fanzine', so the attribution holds within the source.

feature: literal answer to a symbolic question
claim: Asked who or what Oreb is, Wolfe answers only that Oreb is a night chough, declining the symbolic reading the questioner wanted.
quote: Oreb is a night chough.

verdict.trueWording: Oreb is a night chough.
verdict.note: Q1: 'Who or what is Oreb? - Oreb is a night chough.' Quote exact, and the declining-the-symbolic-reading limb is carried by the editorial bracket that follows: 'Needless to say, the questioner hoped for an answer concerning the bird's symbolism or significance....'

feature: answers deferred to the next book
claim: Some questions (Quetzal's motive) are answered only by telling the reader to read the next series, keeping the withholding in force.
quote: You will have to read The Book

verdict.trueWording: You will have to read The Book of the Short Sun.
verdict.note: Q23: 'What was Quetzal's motive in wanting a thriving human colony on Green? - You will have to read The Book of the Short Sun.' The quote fragment is verbatim. That Short Sun is the next series is confirmed lower on the same page: 'It is leading to the Book of the Short Sun. It will deal with the colonists...'

claim: Wolfe reads Tolkien as having uncovered a forgotten Folk Law and built Middle-earth as a means of displaying it in the clearest light, planting the truth that society need not be as we see it.
source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
quote: society need not be as we see it around us

verdict.trueWording: What he did, then, was to plant in my consciousness and yours the truth that society need not be as we see it around us.
verdict.note: Quote exact. Supporting limbs on the page: 'There he found a quality -- let us call it Folk Law -- that has almost disappeared from his world and ours'; 'He uncovered a forgotten wisdom among the barbarian tribes... he had not only uncovered but understood it'; 'Having learned that, he created in Middle-earth a means of displaying it in the clearest and most favourable possible light.' The page's wording is 'created in Middle-earth a means' where the claim says 'built Middle-earth as a means'; the import is the same.

feature: trust the text / do not trust the text
claim: Gaiman's first two rules: trust the text implicitly because the answers are in there, and do not trust it farther than you can throw it because it may go off in your hand.
source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
quote: Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.

verdict.trueWording: 1) Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.
verdict.note: Rule 1 exact. Rule 2 on the page: 'Do not trust the text farther than you can throw it, if that far. It's tricksy and desperate stuff, and it may go off in your hand at any time.' Both limbs of the claim are on the page.

claim: The books subtly reshape themselves while you are away; Peace was a gentle Midwestern memoir on first reading and a horror novel on the second or third.
source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
quote: It only became a horror novel on the second

verdict.trueWording: It only became a horror novel on the second or the third reading.
verdict.note: Rule 3 in full: 'Reread... And anyway, the books will subtly reshape themselves while you are away from them. Peace really was a gentle Midwestern memoir the first time I read it. It only became a horror novel on the second or the third reading.' Quote verbatim; both limbs present.

claim: Wolfe is the kind of clever writer who sees no need to point out his cleverness; the intelligence serves the tale and makes the reader smart too.
source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
quote: He is smart to make you smart as well.

verdict.trueWording: He is smart to make you smart as well.
verdict.note: Rule 7: 'There are two kinds of clever writer. The ones that point out how clever they are, and the ones who see no need to point out how clever they are. Gene Wolfe is of the second kind, and the intelligence is less important than the tale. He is not smart to make you feel stupid. He is smart to make you smart as well.' Quote exact. The claim's 'the intelligence serves the tale' renders the page's 'the intelligence is less important than the tale'.

claim: Rule 8 asserts the author was there and knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror, i.e. the withheld fact is known and recoverable.
source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
quote: He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror

verdict.trueWording: He was there. He saw it happen. He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror that night.
verdict.note: Rule 8 exact, quote verbatim as a prefix. The 'known' limb is rule 8 itself; the 'recoverable' limb is not in rule 8 but is supported elsewhere on the same page by rule 1, 'Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.'

feature: story knows more than it says
claim: Clute's summary law: a Wolfe story always knows more than it says and can almost never be fully grasped on a first reading.
quote: A Wolfe story always knows more than it says

verdict.trueWording: A Wolfe story always knows more than it says, and can almost never be fully grasped on a first-time reading.
verdict.note: Quote exact. The entry is signed '[JC]' - John Clute - and the site footer reads 'Site and SFE content (c) 2011-2026 John Clute & David Langford', so the Clute attribution is supported on the page. The claim writes 'first reading' where the page has 'first-time reading'; the quoted limb itself is untouched by that.

claim: The true story is conveyed by indirection and reveals itself through the reader's ultimate decipherment.
quote: conveyed by indirection

verdict.trueWording: the true story within is generally conveyed by indirection, revealing itself through the reader's ultimate decipherment
verdict.note: SFE (Clute), Archipelago paragraph: 'for although the surface is nearly always described with precision in a Wolfe tale, the true story within is generally conveyed by indirection, revealing itself through the reader's ultimate decipherment and comprehension of the proper and hierarchical sorting of its parts.' Quote verbatim; both limbs on the page; the sentence is framed generally ('in a Wolfe tale'), so the claim's generalisation holds. Fetched raw via curl with a browser UA, HTTP 200.

claim: Fifth Head's clues are almost subliminal on first pass but in retrospect or after rereading lucid and inevitable, and the key twists are extractable from the manuscript that tells the story.
quote: in retrospect or after rereading almost invariably lucid

verdict.trueWording: almost subliminal - but in retrospect or after rereading almost invariably lucid and inevitable - clues
verdict.note: SFE, Fifth Head paragraph, quote verbatim inside 'the almost subliminal - but in retrospect or after rereading almost invariably lucid and inevitable - clues laid down in the text to govern its comprehension.' Second limb also verbatim on the same page: 'the evidence for the transfer (as very frequently in Wolfe) being extractable through an examination of the manuscript that tells the story.' Raw page.

feature: sins of omission with visible gaps
claim: Severian's unreliability is mostly omission; the gaps are not hidden but catch gently on first reading and insistently on rereading.
quote: more sins of omission than outright deception

verdict.trueWording: unreliability often being more sins of omission than outright deception; gaps catch gently, then insistently
verdict.note: Reactor/Evenson, raw page: 'with his unreliability often being more sins of omission than outright deception. There are deliberate gaps in his narrative, but he does little to hide these gaps: they seem meant to catch gently on the reader's attention upon first read, and more insistently as you reread.' Quote verbatim; every limb present.

feature: telling order differs from event order
claim: The rearranged order of recounting, combined with gaps, leaves it uncertain whether Severian hides things or merely tells what he wants in the order he wants, making the unreliability feel human rather than literary.
quote: less literarily motivated, more informal and human

verdict.trueWording: not so much to veil the unreliability as to make it seem less literarily motivated, more informal and human
verdict.note: Same paragraph: 'There's also a significant disjunction in the order in which events happen and the order in which Severian chooses to recount them, and this rearrangement, combined with the gaps, makes it so that it is difficult to say at times ... if Severian is hiding something or simply telling the bits he wants to tell in the order he wants to tell them. That uncertainty is something Wolfe uses not so much to veil the unreliability as to make it seem less literarily motivated, more informal and human.' All limbs verbatim.

claim: Severian's obscure wish to carry the moon-landing picture to a forest reads as random until pages later we learn the moon is now forested; Wolfe often passes such moments in silence.
quote: we later discover that it's exactly right

verdict.trueWording: feels wrong or random to us, when in fact we later discover that it's exactly right
verdict.note: Reactor: Severian 'says that "in some obscure way" he feels he wants to take the picture off the wall and carry it to a mountain forest. Only a few pages later are we told that the moon is now covered with trees ... So Severian's obscure desire to put the moon in the forest feels wrong or random to us, when in fact we later discover that it's exactly right.' The silence limb is also there: 'at least as often Wolfe passes over them in silence.' Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe on the page).

claim: After absorbing Thecla and the Autarch the narrator is a multiplicity speaking as a oneness; a parenthetical memory of torturing for fun turns out to be Thecla's.
quote: a multiplicity trying to speak as if it were a oneness

verdict.trueWording: It is a multiplicity trying to speak as if it were a oneness
verdict.note: Reactor: after the alzabo feast Severian acquires Thecla, and 'Late in the tetralogy Severian encounters the dying Autarch, who encourages him to eat his forebrain ... Severian, once he consumes the Autarch's forebrain, is, in one body, a thousand and two.' Then: 'a multiform and unstable personality is telling a story as if it were stable and unified. It is a multiplicity trying to speak as if it were a oneness.' The parenthetical limb is verbatim too: 'Severian, in a parenthetical, recalls laughing with five other people ... as he plays with torture equipment ... only upon rereading did I realize that he has slipped into Thecla's memories here ... she and her wealthy friends used to sneak into the prison through a secret door and torture people for fun.'

feature: chapter ends in muddle explained next chapter (reader comment)
claim: A commenter observes that chapters tend to end in an incoherent hugger-mugger that the next chapter's opening explains.
quote: explained at the beginning of the next chapter

verdict.trueWording: chapters tend to end with an incoherent hugger-mugger, which is explained at the beginning of the next chapter
verdict.note: Comment thread on the raw page (9 comments were served in the HTML, no JS needed). Attribution confirmed: the comment sits directly under the byline 'NancyLebovitz', 4 years ago. Quote verbatim; the claim's hedge 'tend to' matches the commenter's own 'I think I noticed'.

feature: miracle never acknowledged by the narrator (reader comment)
claim: Commenters note Severian resurrects Dorcas with the Claw and never states that he did so, even after he learns the Claw's power.

verdict.trueWording: never acknowledges the Claw raised Dorcas, though he knows its power
verdict.note: No quote was supplied, so graded on substance. pfsmith: 'Severian indeed "resurrects" Dorcas with the Claw while traveling in the Botanic Gardens ... Severian is clearly aware of the Claw's power to resurrect others, because he uses it for this purpose several times later on. However, it seems very odd that nowhere in the text ... does Severian acknowledge that it was the Claw that raised Dorcas from the lake ... But Severian never explicitly states that he realizes he used the Claw on her.' AndyLove raised it first: 'Severian brings someone back to life accidentally (via the Claw ...) and never figures out that he's done so.' Both attributions verified against the comment bylines. One nuance short of verbatim: AndyLove says Severian never figures it out, pfsmith says he knows the Claw's power but never states it of Dorcas - the claim follows pfsmith.

claim: Wolfe eschews neologism; his obscure real words work at a surface level, a mystery-clue level and an allusive level, which drives close reading and rereading.
quote: Wolfe eschews the use of neologism

verdict.trueWording: prose works on at least three levels: superficial, a story-mystery layer, and an allusive layer
verdict.note: Gerwel/Moher, raw page: 'Wolfe eschews the use of neologism. The words that he uses ... are real English, Greek, or Latinate words, however obscure.' Then: 'its effect is to make the prose work on at least three different levels: There is a superficial meaning ... Below that, there is a deeper meaning which ties to one or another of the story's central mysteries, and below still that there is an allusive layer ...' and 'It is this density of language and its multiplicity of meanings which encourage close readings of Wolfe's texts, and which encourage multiple re-readings of his work.' Every limb verbatim.

claim: Peace never states that its narrator is dead, in a memory-palace purgatory, and probably a multiple murderer; the reader must identify and solve the puzzle from clues.
quote: a puzzle which must be identified and then solved

verdict.trueWording: what Wolfe never states explicitly - a puzzle which must be identified and then solved by the reader's own effort from clues in the text
verdict.note: Gerwel: 'what Wolfe never states explicitly - a puzzle which must be identified and then solved by the reader's own effort from clues in the text - is that the narrator is dead (the story is told by his ghost), that the setting from which he is reminiscing is Purgatory in the form of a memory palace, and that he is in all probability a multiple murderer.' All three unstated premises and the solve-from-clues limb are verbatim.

feature: first sentence paid off by one later line
claim: The opening sentence about the fallen elm becomes clear only when connected to a single, seemingly unrelated line of dialogue in the novel's final third.
quote: a different, single, and seemingly unrelated line

verdict.trueWording: the first sentence ... suddenly becomes clear (when a connection is made to a different, single, and seemingly unrelated line of dialog in the novel's latter third)
verdict.note: Gerwel: 'on re-reading Peace, the significance of individual words (such as a the first sentence "The elm tree planted by Eleanor Bold, the judge's daughter, fell last night.") suddenly becomes clear (when a connection is made to a different, single, and seemingly unrelated line of dialog in the novel's latter third).' Quote verbatim; 'final third' vs the page's 'latter third' is the same sense.

claim: Severian cannot forget yet lies and is inconsistent; Latro cannot remember yet his narrative is consistent, an inversion that asks which narrator is trustworthy.
quote: his narrative is consistent throughout

verdict.trueWording: Latro has an inability to remember anything, yet his narrative is consistent throughout
verdict.note: Gerwel: 'the Latro sequence ... can be read as a inversion of the Book of the New Sun. At the most basic level, Severian has a stated inability to forget anything, though he can choose to lie and is inconsistent in his narrative. While Latro, by contrast, has an inability to remember anything, yet his narrative is consistent throughout. Which story, then, is the more stable? Which narrator the more trustworthy?' Quote verbatim; the inversion and the trustworthiness question are both on the page.

claim: The sentences are clear, cut back and almost Hemingwayesque, while exotic nouns like 'burginot' estrange without obscuring.
